I will run a mainly grain-based plan on 100 mu. In Quzhou County, my baseline is still the winter wheat and summer maize double-cropping system because it matches the local climate, the soils, the machinery I can use efficiently, and the marketing risk I am willing to carry. I do not want a complicated crop mix that raises labor peaks or market uncertainty. I want dependable output, easy mechanization, and a rotation I understand well enough to manage tightly.

So I will keep 80 mu in winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land, and I will put 20 mu into spring peanut. I am keeping peanuts not because I want to transform the farm, but because I want one smaller block that breaks the cereal cycle, spreads risk a little, and improves soil structure and nitrogen balance. Since I am educated and I care about management quality, I will not farm by habit alone. I will control fertilizer more precisely, avoid excessive irrigation, and keep pesticide use tied to field pressure rather than spraying blindly.

For winter wheat, I will use improved seed, aim for stable yield, and manage water carefully because groundwater pressure matters. I will use a moderate but complete fertilizer program with nitrogen as the main driver, plus enough phosphorus and potassium to hold yield and straw strength. I will use plough tillage before wheat establishment where needed to handle residues and create a clean seedbed. I will irrigate a few key times instead of too often, mainly around the stages that matter most for tillering recovery, jointing, and grain filling. I will spray only when disease, aphids, or weeds justify it.

For summer maize, I will use hybrid seed because I want stronger yield potential and more uniform stands. After wheat harvest, I will go with no-tillage seeding on the maize ground to save time, keep moisture, and reduce turnaround pressure during the tight harvest-planting window. I will keep nitrogen high enough to support yield, but I will not overdo it because lodging and wasted cost are real. I will usually irrigate less than wheat, relying on seasonal rain when it comes, and I will keep pesticide passes limited unless armyworm, borers, or weeds require action.

For peanuts, I will use improved seed rather than traditional seed because I want cleaner stand establishment and more even maturity, but I do not need the higher seed cost and tighter management that come with a more specialized strategy. I will use rotary tillage on that block to prepare a lighter, workable seedbed. Fertility there will be more balanced, with less nitrogen and relatively stronger phosphorus and potassium. I will irrigate only enough to secure emergence, pegging, and pod filling if rainfall is short. Pest control will stay moderate.
